text:
By Shelley Shan / Staff reporter, in Amsterdam

Add TT as Preferred Source

China Airlines yesterday completed its showcase flight for its fifth participation in the SkyTeam’s Aviation Challenge, operating a direct flight from Taipei to Amsterdam with sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) equivalent to 40 percent of the flight’s fuel use.

It was the first time the airline had used such a high proportion of SAF on a long-haul flight. In last year’s challenge, it used the same percentage on a regional flight to Bangkok.

China Airlines used a “book and claim” model to raise the SAF use on the Amsterdam flight, which was estimated to reduce carbon dioxide emissions by 93.2 tonnes, equivalent to about one-quarter of the amount absorbed annually by Taipei’s Daan Park, the airline said.

The airline has used SAF on eight flights since 2022, collectively reducing at least 600 tonnes of carbon emissions, China Airlines president Kevin Chen (陳漢銘) said.

“The use of SAF on flights is key to helping the aviation industry transition toward net zero carbon emissions. We are committed to expanding the use of SAF on flights to Europe, North America and Asia, while incorporating low-carbon initiatives into our operations and passenger services,” he said.

The Amsterdam flight also featured several low-carbon initiatives, Chen said.

The airline used tableware in premium business class that is 30 percent lighter than previous versions to help reduce fuel consumption, he said.

The business-class menu and wine list were also printed on recycled paper using soy-based inks, he added.

Passengers were encouraged to check-in online before arriving at the airport and save their boarding passes on their mobile phones instead of printing them on paper, Chen said.

“We send text messages to our members encouraging them to preorder their meals before boarding. This not only helps us better understand passengers’ preferences, but also helps reduce food waste and the fuel required to carry excess food,” he said.

Gourmet plant-based meals developed by Taipei-based Michelin Green Star restaurant Little Tree Food (小小樹食) were served in all classes on the flight, the airline said.

The new Marc Jacobs cobranded travel kits also feature sustainable beauty products and toiletries developed in collaboration with Copenhagen-based design brand FRAMA, it said.

The airline’s Dynasty Sky Reading service has reduced the amount of reading material carried on flights by more than 4,300 tonnes since its introduction, it said.

Meanwhile, the airline expects to receive two Boeing 787-9 aircraft by the end of this year, which are expected to reduce fuel consumption by 20 percent and noise levels by 30 percent, Chen said.

The company aims to have 14 Boeing 787-9 aircraft delivered by the end of next year.

The Taipei-Amsterdam flight was exclusively sponsored by CTBC Bank, which also sponsored China Airlines’ aviation challenge in 2024.

title: Free EU Carbon Allowances Boosted Airline Profits More Than Green Investment, Report Finds
description:
That is the key finding of a new CE Delft report examining free aviation allowances between 2013 and 2025.
Airlines Received €10.9 Billion in Free Allowances The EU originally provided free allowances to airlines to limit competitiveness concerns and reduce the risk of carbon leakage.
The largest benefits came in 2022 and 2023, when airlines continued receiving free allowances while EU carbon prices remained elevated.
Europe Finally Ends Free Airline Allowances The EU has now entered a new phase for aviation carbon pricing.
Under the 2023 EU ETS reforms, free aviation allowances were reduced by 25% in 2024 and 50% in 2025.
text:
European airlines received billions of euros in free carbon allowances under the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), but most of the benefit appears to have supported airline profits rather than new green investment. That is the key finding of a new CE Delft report examining free aviation allowances between 2013 and 2025.

The study estimates airlines received €10.9 billion worth of free EU allowances during the period. By comparison, six major airline groups spent about €1.1 billion on sustainable activities, mainly sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). The findings come as the EU completes its phase-out of free aviation allowances in 2026.

Airlines Received €10.9 Billion in Free Allowances

The EU originally provided free allowances to airlines to limit competitiveness concerns and reduce the risk of carbon leakage. Between 2013 and 2025, airlines received about 350 million free allowances, covering roughly half of the 700 million tonnes of verified aviation emissions reported under the EU ETS during the period.

The value of those allowances increased sharply as carbon prices rose.

CE Delft estimates the average EU allowance price increased from about €4.56 per tonne in 2013 to €73.43 in 2025, measured in 2025 prices. The annual average reached about €87.90 per tonne in 2022.

That made free allowances increasingly valuable to airlines, particularly during the years when carbon prices were high. The largest benefits came in 2022 and 2023, when airlines continued receiving free allowances while EU carbon prices remained elevated.

The author noted:

“We find no strong reason to expect that these expenditures would have been substantially lower without free allocation. EU ETS auction revenues, on the other hand, are largely used for climate and energy transition purposes. Full auctioning of aviation allowances would therefore most likely have made significantly more funding available for the decarbonisation of the European economy.”

Free Allocation Became a Major Profit Booster

CE Delft compared airline profitability with a scenario in which airlines had to purchase all their EU allowances. The six airline groups studied were Ryanair, Lufthansa, Air France-KLM, easyJet, Wizz Air and IAG.

For five major European airline groups that were profitable over the period, the report estimates that free allocation accounted for about 17% of profitability. For Air France-KLM, which recorded cumulative losses, free allowances reduced those losses by about 10%.

The report also finds little evidence that ending free allocation has seriously damaged airline profitability. European airline margins during 2023–2025 were broadly comparable with pre-pandemic levels, even as free allocation declined sharply.

That does not mean airlines would face no costs from buying all their allowances. But it weakens the argument that free allocation was essential to protect the sector’s financial performance.

RELATED: Top 5 Airports Driving Global Aviation Emissions as Expansion Fuels Climate Risks

Green Spending Fell Far Behind the Carbon Windfall

The biggest concern raised by the report is the gap between the value of free allowances and spending on sustainable activities. The six airline groups spent approximately €80 million on sustainable capital investments during the period studied.

They also spent an estimated €1 billion on SAF purchases. Combined, that is roughly €1.1 billion, compared with the €10.9 billion estimated value of free carbon allowances.

CE Delft also examined 2025 EU Taxonomy reporting from eight airlines. The airlines reported a combined €18.1 billion in capital expenditure. About €9.57 billion, or 52.8%, was classified as taxonomy-aligned.

However, almost all of that spending — €9.55 billion — was classified as transitional activity, mainly conventional aircraft purchases and maintenance.

Only €24 million, or 0.13% of total reported capital expenditure, was classified as genuinely sustainable investment. This consisted of electric ground-handling equipment reported by Air France-KLM.

The distinction matters because newer aircraft can use less fuel than older models but still rely mainly on fossil-based jet fuel.

Could Auction Revenue Have Delivered More?

The report argues that governments could have used auction revenue to support technologies that can cut aviation emissions. CE Delft models several hypothetical uses for the €10.9 billion in free allowances.

If the money had instead been used to purchase HEFA-based SAF, the report estimates it could have supported about 18 million tonnes of CO₂ reductions. Using synthetic SAF could have produced about 4.7 million tonnes of reductions.

The report also estimates that putting the money into the EU Innovation Fund could theoretically have generated up to 815 million tonnes of reductions across sectors. These are not actual historical savings. They are illustrative scenarios based on different technology and investment assumptions.

Still, they highlight the potential opportunity cost of giving carbon allowances to airlines rather than auctioning them.

The wider EU ETS has already become a major source of climate funding. EU ETS auctions generated more than €258 billion between 2013 and 2025, with revenues exceeding €43 billion in 2025, according to the European Commission.

Aviation’s Carbon Costs Remain Partly Unpriced

The report also examines aviation’s wider climate impact. For the six airline groups, CE Delft estimates their external climate costs reached almost €30 billion in 2025.

That included about €14.7 billion from direct aircraft CO₂ emissions, €4.6 billion from fuel-production emissions and €10.3 billion from non-CO₂ climate effects. These figures show why aviation’s climate impact extends beyond the CO₂ covered by the EU ETS.

CE Delft estimates that carbon pricing has internalized around 40% of the external cost of direct CO₂ emissions within the EU ETS scope in recent years. But the picture changes when international aviation and non-CO₂ effects are included.

For 2025, the report estimates only 16% of CO₂-related external costs were internalized when intercontinental aviation was included. Non-CO₂ effects, including climate impacts linked to aircraft emissions at altitude, remain much less covered by carbon pricing.

Europe Finally Ends Free Airline Allowances

The EU has now entered a new phase for aviation carbon pricing. Under the 2023 EU ETS reforms, free aviation allowances were reduced by 25% in 2024 and 50% in 2025. From 2026, regular free allocation has ended, and aviation allowances are auctioned.

The change means airlines now face a clearer market-based carbon cost for their EU ETS emissions. At the same time, the EU is directing carbon market resources toward aviation decarbonization.

Between 2024 and 2030, up to 20 million EU ETS allowances will be used to help narrow the cost gap between eligible SAF and conventional jet fuel.

EASA expects aviation emissions covered by the EU ETS to reach about 59.5 million tonnes in 2026. It estimates airlines could need to purchase about 34.5 million allowances this year. That makes the price of carbon increasingly important to airline costs.

The Next Test for Aviation Carbon Policy

The CE Delft report does not show that free allowances had no value to airlines. Instead, it raises a broader question about whether the policy delivered enough climate benefits for its cost.

The report was commissioned by Opportunity Green, so its policy recommendations should be considered in that context. Its analysis, however, uses EU ETS data, airline financial reports, EU Taxonomy disclosures and other published datasets.

With free allocation now ending, the focus shifts to what happens next. A stronger carbon price can increase the cost of flying while creating revenue for climate investment.

The challenge for Europe is to ensure that those revenues help scale technologies such as SAF, synthetic fuels, and eventually hydrogen and electric aviation.

For the EU’s carbon market, the goal is no longer simply putting a price on aviation emissions. It is turning that price into measurable progress toward cleaner flight.

title: Bangchak Group at APPEC 2026 in Singapore
description:

For Bangchak Group, this means connecting its energy resources and two refineries with trading, logistics and risk management, so it can adjust supply and delivery as conditions change.
Investment in core businesses and low-carbon energy is also not an either-or choice.
Both drew strong interest, reflecting rising demand for low-carbon fuels in aviation, transportation and hard-to-abate industries.
Bangchak Group’s participation in APPEC 2026 and IFFW Singapore Brief 2026 reflected its focus on Energy Security and Resiliency alongside the development of low-carbon fuels.
text:
Bangchak Group joined more than 1,200 policymakers, senior executives, industry experts and technology developers from 55 countries at the 42nd Asia Pacific Petroleum Conference (APPEC 2026) in Singapore, organized by S&P Global Energy. As an event sponsor, the Group contributed to discussions on the outlook for Asia-Pacific oil markets, shifts in global supply and the future of the energy transition.

In an Executive Interview with Mr. Rob Westervelt, Head of Content at S&P Global Energy Events, Mr. Chaiwat Kovavisarach, Group Chief Executive Officer and President of Bangchak Corporation Public Company Limited, shared his perspective on running an energy business at a time when volatility has become the norm. The real challenge, he said, is not getting every market call right. It is building a business that can continue to source, process and deliver energy when the unexpected happens. For Bangchak Group, this means connecting its energy resources and two refineries with trading, logistics and risk management, so it can adjust supply and delivery as conditions change. Investment in core businesses and low-carbon energy is also not an either-or choice. Both are needed to secure today’s energy supply and create options for the future.

Mr. Chaiwat was also interviewed by Mr. Mayank Maheshwari, Equity Analyst, Morgan Stanley Asia (Singapore) Pte., for Morgan Stanley’s internal media under the theme “In Conversation with the CEO,” covering fuel market conditions, government policy, the global refining outlook and Bangchak Group’s capital allocation.

Mr. Bundit Hansapaiboon, President, Refinery and Marketing Business Group, Bangchak Corporation Plc., delivered a keynote presentation on “Asia Refining Outlook – Capacity, Competition, and Margins.” He said competitive refineries need to manage the full value chain - from diversifying crude supply and improving efficiency and asset utilization to linking trading with logistics and adapting products to market demand. They must do so while balancing energy security, affordable prices and environmental sustainability. Mr. Bundit also showed how existing refinery infrastructure can be used to produce future fuels. Bangchak’s facility can switch between sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO) based on market demand, using the existing logistics system.

The Group also showcased its low-carbon products at the event, particularly SAF and HVO. Both drew strong interest, reflecting rising demand for low-carbon fuels in aviation, transportation and hard-to-abate industries.

During the same week, Mrs. Gloyta Nathalang, Senior Executive Vice President, Sustainability Management and Corporate Communications, Bangchak Corporation Plc., joined a panel at IFFW Singapore Brief 2026, organized by International Future Fuels Week, on “Building Bankable Future Fuel Markets Across Asia-Pacific.” The discussion underscored the importance of feedstock management. Panelists noted that market forces alone will not scale SAF and other low-carbon fuels to the level required. Clear policies, blending mandates and long-term offtake agreements are needed to create demand certainty and make projects bankable. Infrastructure is another major gap: the value chain must work as one connected system, from feedstock through to fuel use.

Bangchak Group’s participation in APPEC 2026 and IFFW Singapore Brief 2026 reflected its focus on Energy Security and Resiliency alongside the development of low-carbon fuels. This brings together capabilities across energy resources, refining, trading and logistics, infrastructure, technology and markets to meet today’s energy needs and support the longer-term energy transition.

text:
Akasa Air, India’s fastest-growing airline, successfully operated a commercial flight using conventional aviation turbine fuel blended with 1% sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), supplied by Bharat Petroleum Corp. Ltd. (BPCL) on Sept. 8, 2026. The flight departed Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport, Mumbai, at 13:05hrs IST and arrived at Manohar International Airport (GOX), Goa, at 14:30hrs IST.

The initiative builds on the Memorandum of Understanding signed by Akasa Air and BPCL in July 2026 to explore adoption of SAF, along with other opportunities supporting aviation decarbonization. The flight will provide both organizations with insights and practical learnings that can help inform future initiatives.

Commenting on the milestone, Ankur Goel, chief financial officer, Akasa Air, said, “Sustainability is one of Akasa Air’s core values and shapes how we are building the airline for the long term. Since inception, we have invested in next-generation aircraft, technology and responsible practices that enable more conscious and efficient operations, both on the ground and in the air. This flight with BPCL translates our partnership into tangible action. Scaling SAF in India will require coordinated action across the ecosystem, supported by domestic supply, enabling policy and commercial viability. We are committed to exploring this transition.”

Subhankar Sen, director (marketing), Bharat Petroleum Corp. Ltd. (BPCL), said, “The transition from conventional fuels to sustainable alternatives is both an environmental imperative and a strategic necessity for India. While feedstock availability and aggregation have historically posed challenges due to fragmented supply chains, sustained efforts across the value chain have helped create the foundation for a viable Sustainable Aviation Fuel ecosystem. BPCL remains firmly committed to advancing sustainable fuels as part of India's broader energy transition journey. As a nation that relies significantly on crude oil imports, enhancing energy security through sustainable and indigenous energy solutions is the way forward. BPCL is actively driving sustainability initiatives across multiple sectors, and today's milestone with Akasa Air marks an important step in extending these efforts to aviation and supporting India's decarbonization goals. He also thanked the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, the Ministry of Civil Aviation, and DGCA for their unwavering support and guidance in making this achievement possible.”

The flight comes as India works towards its ambition of achieving 5% SAF blending by 2030 and reflects the aviation industry’s broader focus on reducing carbon emissions. It also contributes to the International Air Transport Association’s goal of achieving net-zero carbon emissions by 2050.

Sustainability has been embedded in Akasa Air’s ethos since inception, with the airline continuing to implement initiatives focused on conscious and efficient operations.

Akasa Air’s brand-new Boeing 737 MAX fleet is a key enabler of its mission to operate one of the most environmentally progressive and fuel-efficient fleets in the Indian skies. Powered by CFM International LEAP-1B engines and incorporating advanced-technology winglets, the 737 MAX offers excellent economics, reducing fuel use and emissions by 20 per cent compared to the airplanes it replaces. The airline has also partnered with OpenAirlines to implement SkyBreathe, a cutting-edge fuel management solution that uses advanced analytics to reduce carbon emissions and enhance operational efficiency across the network. Akasa Air was the first Indian airline to voluntarily opt out of traditional water-cannon salutes at route inaugurations, conserving over 5,50,000 liters of water to date.

text:
The SAF Global Summit 2026 will take place on 22 and 23 September at the QEII Centre in London, bringing together airlines, governments, fuel producers, airports, investors and technology companies to address the scaling of sustainable aviation fuel. The United Kingdom and Canada are among the countries participating.

Organisers expect more than 1,000 attendees and over 150 speakers, including senior decision-makers from aviation, energy, government and finance. The two-day programme covers policy, investment, production, supply chains and infrastructure, including a dedicated session on bridging the "last-mile to wing-tip" challenge of getting SAF from production to aircraft. A SAF Market & Trade Forum will cover investment structures, demand signals and trading mechanisms, reflecting a shift toward treating SAF as a strategic commodity rather than solely an environmental product.

Discussions are expected to address policy frameworks including the ReFuelEU Aviation regulation, the UK SAF Mandate and US policy incentives, along with how long-term offtake agreements between airlines and producers can underpin investment decisions and how commercial-scale SAF facilities can reach final investment decisions. SAF can be produced from renewable and waste-based feedstocks and blended with conventional jet fuel for use in existing aircraft, though high production costs and supply chain complexity remain significant barriers to large-scale adoption.

title: Yusen Logistics signs multi-year SAF agreement with Finnair - Container News
description:
Yusen Logistics and Finnair have signed a multi-year agreement covering Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) environmental attributes.
Agreement uses Book-and-Claim model Under the agreement, Yusen Logistics will purchase SAF-related environmental attributes from Finnair.
Yusen targets air freight emissions Yusen Logistics said the agreement will provide customers with another option to address emissions from their air freight operations.
Finnair looks to strengthen SAF demand Finnair said the multi-year agreement can help create longer-term demand for SAF.

text:
Yusen Logistics and Finnair have signed a multi-year agreement covering Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) environmental attributes.

The partnership aims to reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions linked to air cargo transportation.

Agreement uses Book-and-Claim model

Under the agreement, Yusen Logistics will purchase SAF-related environmental attributes from Finnair.

The companies will use a Book-and-Claim mechanism. This allows the environmental benefits of SAF to be allocated separately from the physical movement of the fuel and cargo.

As a result, customers can support SAF use even when the fuel is not physically used on their specific shipment.

Participating customers may also receive certificates and emissions-related reports linked to their allocated SAF environmental attributes.

Yusen targets air freight emissions

Yusen Logistics said the agreement will provide customers with another option to address emissions from their air freight operations.

“Our customers increasingly expect tangible and credible solutions to reduce the environmental impact of their supply chains,” said Eisuke Fukagawa, Head of Air Freight Forwarding Unit at Yusen Logistics Global Management.

He added that the Book-and-Claim model can provide customers with greater transparency through certificates and emissions reporting.

Finnair looks to strengthen SAF demand

Finnair said the multi-year agreement can help create longer-term demand for SAF.

“This multi-year agreement with Yusen Logistics is an important milestone in reducing the climate impact of air cargo,” said Gabriela Hiitola, Senior Vice President of Finnair Cargo.

The agreement was concluded with support from Western Associates, Finnair’s General Sales Agent in Japan.

text:
BRICS countries have backed greater cooperation on sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) and low-carbon aviation fuels while advancing new frameworks for transport decarbonisation, urban mobility and logistics cooperation.

The commitments were included in the BRICS New Delhi Declaration 2026, adopted during the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12–13. The declaration links transport cooperation with broader objectives around sustainable development, resilient infrastructure and environmental sustainability.

The transport measures include support for a BRICS Forum on Sustainable Aviation Fuels, a framework for exchanging knowledge on transport decarbonisation and the establishment of a BRICS Urban Mobility Hub. The declaration also welcomed a logistics supply-chain cooperation framework and encouraged further discussion on a proposed BRICS Railway Research Network.

BRICS puts SAF on the transport cooperation agenda

The declaration specifically recognises sustainable aviation fuels and low-carbon aviation fuels as tools for reducing carbon emissions from international aviation.

The commitment places SAF within a wider BRICS transport cooperation agenda covering policy, investment, technology and capacity building. Member countries said these areas would help develop sustainable and resilient transport infrastructure while recognising the importance of transport to economic growth, connectivity and environmental sustainability.

The proposed BRICS Forum on Sustainable Aviation Fuels could provide a platform for member countries to exchange knowledge and coordinate on issues associated with SAF development. However, the declaration does not set out specific production targets, investment commitments or timelines for SAF deployment.

For the aviation sector, the significance of the declaration therefore lies primarily in establishing a multilateral framework for cooperation rather than announcing a specific SAF programme.

Transport decarbonisation and renewable energy

BRICS members also welcomed a framework for cooperation on exchanging knowledge related to transport decarbonisation.

The declaration calls for this cooperation to leverage the renewable energy potential of BRICS countries, connecting transport decarbonisation with the wider expansion of clean energy. It also highlights the importance of incorporating circular economy principles into the development and maintenance of transport infrastructure.

This approach broadens the role of renewable energy in the transport transition beyond individual fuels or technologies. For countries with significant renewable energy resources, closer knowledge-sharing could support the development of lower-carbon transport systems while allowing national priorities and circumstances to shape implementation.

The declaration also reaffirmed the importance of transport policy, investment, technological cooperation and capacity building.

Urban mobility and logistics frameworks

Alongside aviation, BRICS is seeking deeper cooperation in urban transport.

The BRICS Urban Mobility Hub is intended to support knowledge exchange and cooperation around accessible, affordable, inclusive and smart urban transport solutions. The declaration also welcomed the outcomes of the BRICS Urbanisation Forum and highlighted cooperation on sustainable mobility and other urban services.

In logistics, BRICS welcomed the establishment of a Logistics Supply-Chain Cooperation Framework with the intention to strengthen cooperation across transport and supply-chain systems as the grouping seeks more resilient and efficient connectivity.

The declaration further encouraged discussion on the proposal for a BRICS Railway Research Network, adding rail research and knowledge-sharing to the grouping’s growing transport agenda.

Broader cooperation across the transport sector

The transport commitments form part of a broader BRICS effort to strengthen infrastructure cooperation among member countries.

The declaration welcomed further transport dialogue, including in civil aviation, while emphasising cooperation that respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of member states. It also reaffirmed the importance of developing sustainable and resilient transport infrastructure.

For the SAF industry, the inclusion of aviation fuels alongside urban mobility, logistics and rail research indicates that BRICS is treating transport decarbonisation as a multi-sector issue rather than a standalone aviation initiative.

Implementation will determine impact

The New Delhi Declaration provides political backing for deeper cooperation on sustainable transport, but the next stage will be implementation.

The proposed SAF forum, transport decarbonisation framework, Urban Mobility Hub and logistics framework could create channels for sharing technology, policy experience and project knowledge across BRICS countries. The proposed Railway Research Network could similarly extend cooperation into rail transport.

For the aviation sector, the immediate outcome is a stronger multilateral endorsement of SAF and low-carbon aviation fuels. Turning that commitment into measurable emissions reductions will require individual countries and industry participants to develop concrete projects, investment structures, supply chains and policy mechanisms.

Bioenergy Business Analysis

The BRICS commitment to promote SAF and low-carbon aviation fuels provides a new multilateral platform for cooperation among major emerging economies, many of which have substantial renewable energy, agricultural and industrial resources that could contribute to future low-carbon fuel value chains.

However, the declaration remains a framework for cooperation rather than a binding SAF deployment plan. It does not establish collective production volumes, financing mechanisms, blending mandates or individual country targets. The practical impact will depend on whether the proposed SAF forum translates knowledge exchange into project development, technology cooperation, investment and compatible policy frameworks.

The wider transport agenda could nevertheless be significant for renewable fuels and infrastructure. Linking SAF with renewable energy cooperation, circular economy principles, logistics and urban mobility creates opportunities for BRICS members to address transport emissions across several segments while developing domestic clean-energy industries.

text:
GEVO, Inc. (NASDAQ: GEVO) today announced continued progress on the debottlenecking initiative at its GEVO North Dakota ("GND") facility in Richardton, North Dakota, including the successful commissioning of a new beer degassing system ahead of schedule which will capture and sequester more CO₂. The debottlenecking will result in a 10-15 percent increase in GND output and returns and closely follows the successful commissioning of a steam turbine project in August.

The debottlenecking program is designed to enhance operating efficiency and increase production capacity at GND as the facility advances toward its targeted production capacity of approximately 75 million gallons per year. The project includes three primary upgrades:

Addition of a third liquefaction tank to expand capacity and improve the yield of corn starch to sugars

Addition of a fifth fermenter to increase fermentation residence time to enable the production of more ethanol and CO₂

Installation of a beer degassing system to capture and sequester additional CO₂ from the ethanol process

The CO₂ beer degassing system is currently being commissioned, several weeks earlier than originally planned. This equipment will enable GND to increase CO₂ recovery, unlock distillation capacity, and lower the facility CI score.

"This milestone represents another step forward in our efforts to optimize GND and unlock additional value from an already strong operating asset," said Gevo Chief Executive Officer Paul Bloom. "Our debottlenecking program is focused on practical, high-return improvements that enhance production efficiency, carbon capture performance and overall facility economics."

Construction and installation activities associated with liquefaction and fermentation continue to progress on schedule and both assets are expected to be operational by the end of 2026.

GND also recently completed the commissioning of a steam turbine project. The project lowers the plant energy consumption by optimizing the steam usage inside the plant while lowering the amount of purchased electricity. This project was already started prior to Gevo's acquisition of the facility and was successfully integrated into plant operations in August.

The steam turbine and debottlenecking project are both examples of Gevo's ability to unlock process capacity while operating safely and efficiently. These projects are laying the groundwork for the planned 75Mgpy expansion of GND which is anticipated to approximately double the output and returns from GND and is expected to be completed in 2028.

About Gevo

Gevo is a next-generation diversified energy company committed to fueling America's future with cost-effective, drop-in fuels that contribute to energy security, abate carbon, and strengthen rural communities to drive economic growth. Gevo's innovative technology can be used to make a variety of renewable products, including sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), motor fuels, chemicals, and other materials that provide U.S.-made solutions. Gevo's business model includes developing, financing, and operating production facilities that create jobs and revitalize communities. Gevo owns and operates an ethanol plant with an adjacent carbon capture and storage (CCS) facility and Class VI carbon-storage well. Gevo also owns and operates one of the largest dairy-based renewable natural gas (RNG) facilities in the United States, turning by-products into clean, reliable energy. Additionally, Gevo developed the world's first production facility for specialty alcohol-to-jet (ATJ) fuels and chemicals operating since 2012. Gevo is currently developing the world's first large-scale ATJ facility to be co-located at our North Dakota site. Gevo's market-driven "pay-for-performance" approach regarding carbon and other sustainability attributes helps deliver value to our local economies. Through its Verity subsidiary, Gevo provides transparency, accountability, and efficiency in tracking, measuring, and verifying various attributes throughout the supply chain. By strengthening rural economies, Gevo is working to secure a self-sufficient future and to make sure value is brought to the market.

text:
Akasa Air, India’s fastest-growing airline, successfully operated a commercial flight using conventional aviation turbine fuel blended with 1% sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), supplied by Bharat Petroleum Corp. Ltd. (BPCL) on Sept. 8, 2026. The flight departed Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport, Mumbai, at 13:05hrs IST and arrived at Manohar International Airport (GOX), Goa, at 14:30hrs IST.

The initiative builds on the Memorandum of Understanding signed by Akasa Air and BPCL in July 2026 to explore adoption of SAF, along with other opportunities supporting aviation decarbonization. The flight will provide both organizations with insights and practical learnings that can help inform future initiatives.

Commenting on the milestone, Ankur Goel, chief financial officer, Akasa Air, said, “Sustainability is one of Akasa Air’s core values and shapes how we are building the airline for the long term. Since inception, we have invested in next-generation aircraft, technology and responsible practices that enable more conscious and efficient operations, both on the ground and in the air. This flight with BPCL translates our partnership into tangible action. Scaling SAF in India will require coordinated action across the ecosystem, supported by domestic supply, enabling policy and commercial viability. We are committed to exploring this transition.”

Subhankar Sen, director (marketing), Bharat Petroleum Corp. Ltd. (BPCL), said, “The transition from conventional fuels to sustainable alternatives is both an environmental imperative and a strategic necessity for India. While feedstock availability and aggregation have historically posed challenges due to fragmented supply chains, sustained efforts across the value chain have helped create the foundation for a viable Sustainable Aviation Fuel ecosystem. BPCL remains firmly committed to advancing sustainable fuels as part of India's broader energy transition journey. As a nation that relies significantly on crude oil imports, enhancing energy security through sustainable and indigenous energy solutions is the way forward. BPCL is actively driving sustainability initiatives across multiple sectors, and today's milestone with Akasa Air marks an important step in extending these efforts to aviation and supporting India's decarbonization goals. He also thanked the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, the Ministry of Civil Aviation, and DGCA for their unwavering support and guidance in making this achievement possible.”

The flight comes as India works towards its ambition of achieving 5% SAF blending by 2030 and reflects the aviation industry’s broader focus on reducing carbon emissions. It also contributes to the International Air Transport Association’s goal of achieving net-zero carbon emissions by 2050.

Sustainability has been embedded in Akasa Air’s ethos since inception, with the airline continuing to implement initiatives focused on conscious and efficient operations.

Akasa Air’s brand-new Boeing 737 MAX fleet is a key enabler of its mission to operate one of the most environmentally progressive and fuel-efficient fleets in the Indian skies. Powered by CFM International LEAP-1B engines and incorporating advanced-technology winglets, the 737 MAX offers excellent economics, reducing fuel use and emissions by 20 per cent compared to the airplanes it replaces. The airline has also partnered with OpenAirlines to implement SkyBreathe, a cutting-edge fuel management solution that uses advanced analytics to reduce carbon emissions and enhance operational efficiency across the network. Akasa Air was the first Indian airline to voluntarily opt out of traditional water-cannon salutes at route inaugurations, conserving over 5,50,000 liters of water to date.

text:
Dickow Pumpen has been manufacturing high-performance industrial pumps since 1910. Based in Germany, the company was re-established in Waldkraiburg, Bavaria, after World War II. Dickow Pumpen’s engineering, manufacturing and innovation activities are still based there today. The company has been evolving for more than a century into a globally active specialist in demanding centrifugal pump applications.

“Our pumps are used in critical industries ranging from chemicals, petrochemicals and energy to emerging sectors such as sustainable fuels, environmental technologies and data centres,” says Alexander Hammer, Managing Director of Dickow Pumpen. “As a medium-sized company with customers worldwide, we continue to invest heavily in our Waldkraiburg site through our long-term Future-Fit programme, strengthening our production, testing and logistics capabilities.”

Today, the business is owned by the Astrid Dickow Foundation, allowing its leadership to think and invest for the long term rather than focusing on short-term shareholder expectations. This commitment to quality, sustainability and customer partnership is reflected in the fact that many Dickow pumps remain in operation for several decades.

“Pumps are far more important than most people realise. You cannot decarbonise industry without moving, processing and storing liquids safely and efficiently,” Hammer tells us. “Whether it is Sustainable Aviation Fuel, renewable energy, chemical processing or environmental technology, reliable pump systems are an essential enabling technology.”

Dickow supports these industries with engineering expertise, long-term partnerships and solutions that help customers achieve both operational and sustainability goals.

As Hammer says, “In many ways, the energy transition will be built not only with new energy sources, but also with reliable infrastructure working quietly in the background.”

Dickow Pumpen does not sell pumps off the shelf. Every Dickow pump is engineered for a specific application and tailored to the customer’s exact process requirements.

The Best Product and the Best Support

“We focus on understanding the complete operating environment, including the fluid, the process, safety requirements, efficiency targets and maintenance expectations,” Hammer explains. “We don’t see ourselves as a pump supplier, but as a long-term engineering partner for critical industrial processes.”

These pumps are designed and built to operate in demanding and safety-critical applications involving hazardous media, high temperatures, high pressures or continuous operation. That is where Dickow’s expertise in magnetically coupled sealless pumps, high-temperature pumps and other specialised designs creates real value. Rather than optimising for the lowest purchase price, the firm focuses on reliability, availability and minimising the total cost of ownership over the entire lifecycle of the equipment.

“What truly differentiates us, however, is our commitment beyond the product itself. Our relationship with the customer does not end when a pump leaves the factory,” Hammer points out. “We provide commissioning support, spare parts, maintenance services, and technical training through the Dickow Academy, and ongoing engineering assistance throughout the entire lifecycle of the pump.”

Continuous Improvement

Through digital services, documentation platforms and future condition-monitoring solutions, Dickow also helps customers maximise reliability and operational performance. This is essential in an era where customers are under increasing pressure to improve energy efficiency, reduce emissions and comply with stricter environmental regulations.

“As a pump manufacturer, this means we must continuously improve our products and support customers in achieving both operational and sustainability objectives,” Hammer says. “Digitalisation is another important area. Traditional mechanical engineering companies must combine decades of engineering expertise with new digital technologies, data-driven services and modern development tools.”

This requires investments not only in technology, but also in people, processes and skills. Ultimately, the challenge is to balance continuous investment in innovation, production capabilities and future technologies with long-term profitability and competitiveness.

“We see this not only as a challenge, but also as an opportunity to strengthen our position as a specialised engineering partner for demanding industrial applications,” says Hammer. “We have addressed these challenges by consistently investing in our people, our technology and our production capabilities rather than trying to compete on price alone. As a specialist for demanding pump applications, our strategy has always been to differentiate ourselves through engineering expertise, reliability and customer value.”

Over the years, Dickow has continuously strengthened its production infrastructure, testing capabilities and manufacturing processes while maintaining a high level of in-house manufacturing expertise.

“It gives us greater control over quality, flexibility and delivery performance. This has helped us remain resilient even during periods of supply-chain disruption and market uncertainty,” Hammer explains. “Another important factor has been our close collaboration with customers and suppliers. By understanding industry trends and future requirements early, we can adapt our products and technologies to new process conditions and changing market needs.”

Built on Talent

The most valuable assets in overcoming all of these challenges are Dickow’s employees, and Hammer is clear that attracting and retaining talented people requires much more than simply filling vacancies.

“We focus on creating an environment where people can develop professionally, take responsibility and build long-term careers,” says Hammer. “Machines can be purchased, but expertise has to be developed over years and sometimes decades. That is why investing in people is one of the most important investments we make as a company.”

A key pillar of Dickow’s approach is investing in young talent. It does this by maintaining a strong apprenticeship programme, cooperating closely with regional schools, universities and training institutions, and offering apprenticeship and dual-study opportunities.

“For us, developing talent internally is often the most sustainable way to build the specialised engineering and manufacturing expertise our industry requires,” Hammer says.

That is why learning does not stop for Dickow’s people after they join the company. Dickow invests continuously in technical training, leadership development and cross-departmental knowledge sharing.

“Our culture is very hands-on, and we encourage employees to learn from real projects, collaborate across functions and contribute their own ideas for improvements and innovation,” Hammer explains. “We strongly believe in promoting from within whenever possible and offering long-term development opportunities. In fact, I, as Managing Director, started my career as an apprentice and worked my way through different positions to lead the company today.”

As for tomorrow, Dickow Pumpen has made its plans around three key areas – innovation, sustainability, and digitalisation.

“We see strong growth opportunities in sustainable fuels, renewable energy and environmental technologies, where reliable pump systems are essential for the decarbonisation of industry,” says Hammer. “At the same time, we continue to invest in our production facilities, testing capabilities and digital services such as condition monitoring, digital documentation and future digital twin concepts. As a foundation-owned company, we can focus on long-term investments and sustainable growth while continuing to provide the reliability, engineering expertise and customer support that have defined Dickow for more than a century.”

title: KLM Cityhopper Marks 60 Years with 58 Aircraft, 80+ Destinations and 350 Daily Flights
authors: Dell Galen, • Jake Adams, • Dell Galen
description:

Around 11 million passengers travel with KLM Cityhopper each year.
Recent additions to the KLM Cityhopper network include Biarritz, Exeter, Dubrovnik, Ljubljana, Cork, Jersey, Santiago de Compostela and Oviedo.
Further consolidation followed with a merger with NetherLines in 1991 and the later integration of KLM UK, eventually creating the KLM Cityhopper operation known today.
KLM Cityhopper has also introduced OptiClimb, a system designed to reduce fuel consumption and CO₂ emissions during an aircraft’s climb to cruising altitude.
text:
KLM Cityhopper is celebrating its 60th anniversary, marking six decades of growth from a small domestic airline operating two leased Fokker aircraft to one of the key components of KLM’s European network.

Today, the regional carrier operates a fleet of 58 aircraft, serves more than 80 destinations and runs over 350 flights per day. Around 11 million passengers travel with KLM Cityhopper each year.

Its operations are closely integrated with KLM’s hub at Amsterdam Airport Schiphol, feeding passengers from cities across Europe into the airline’s long-haul network while also connecting international arrivals with destinations throughout the continent.

Recent additions to the KLM Cityhopper network include Biarritz, Exeter, Dubrovnik, Ljubljana, Cork, Jersey, Santiago de Compostela and Oviedo.

“Sixty years ago, KLM Cityhopper began as a small regional airline. Today, we are an essential part of KLM’s network and play a key role in connecting Europe with the world,” said Maarten Koopmans, Managing Director of KLM Cityhopper.

From NLM to KLM Cityhopper

The airline’s history dates back to 1966, when Nederlandse Luchtvaart Maatschappij, or NLM, was established to provide faster air connections between regions of the Netherlands.

Operations initially began with two leased Fokker aircraft and a limited domestic network. Over the following decades, the airline gradually expanded beyond the Netherlands and added destinations across Europe.

The Cityhopper name was introduced in 1976. Further consolidation followed with a merger with NetherLines in 1991 and the later integration of KLM UK, eventually creating the KLM Cityhopper operation known today.

The airline continued to operate aircraft produced by Dutch manufacturer Fokker for several decades before beginning its transition to Embraer aircraft in 2008.

Embraer fleet at the centre of operations

Embraer aircraft now form the backbone of KLM Cityhopper’s fleet, including the latest-generation E195-E2.

The E195-E2 offers lower fuel consumption and noise levels than previous-generation regional aircraft, supporting KLM Cityhopper’s efforts to improve the efficiency of its short-haul operations.

Fleet development will remain one of the airline’s priorities as it looks to further optimise its network and add new European destinations.

KLM Cityhopper used to test new aviation technology

Beyond its role as KLM’s regional operator, Cityhopper has increasingly been used as a testing ground for technologies and operational changes that could later be adopted more widely across the KLM group.

Among these initiatives is virtual reality training for pilots, which supplements conventional simulator and in-flight training.

KLM Cityhopper has also introduced OptiClimb, a system designed to reduce fuel consumption and CO₂ emissions during an aircraft’s climb to cruising altitude.

The application analyses factors including aircraft weight, weather, aircraft type and route before recommending an optimised climb speed to the flight crew.

The carrier is also participating in The Aviation Challenge for a fourth year, testing initiatives involving artificial intelligence, sustainable aviation fuel, aircraft weight reduction, reduced food waste and the electrification of ground operations.

Six decades after its first flights, KLM Cityhopper has evolved from a small domestic operation into a major feeder airline for one of Europe’s largest aviation hubs, linking KLM’s long-haul network at Schiphol with more than 80 destinations across Europe.

text:
In his address, he said producing sustainable fuels through power-to-liquids technology remains constrained by costs, efficiency limits, and the difficulty of scaling scientific discoveries into commercially viable projects.

The sub-forum is part of the 19th Pujiang Innovation Forum in Shanghai, China, where South African and international researchers, policymakers and business representatives gathered to discuss innovation and technological cooperation.

South Africa is this year’s Country of Honour, with the Minister of Science, Technology and Innovation, Professor Blade Nzimande, leading the South African delegation.

Breaking the barriers

“These challenges are precisely where research and innovation can create value. I invite the next generation of scientists and engineers to help us address them,” Mudzunga said.

He added that power-to-liquids technology could allow Sasol to combine renewable electricity, green hydrogen and captured carbon dioxide to produce sustainable liquid fuels.

While Sasol’s decades of experience in synthetic-fuel production gave it an advantage, significant scientific and commercial obstacles remain.

“We need further innovation throughout the process. We must improve hydrogen efficiency, achieve higher conversion efficiency, increase yields and reduce overall costs — particularly the cost of green hydrogen, which remains very high.”

Mudzunga warned that scientific breakthroughs alone would not drive the energy transition. Universities, government, research institutions and companies needed to collaborate from early research through to commercial deployment.

“At the research end, we work closely with universities, government and other organisations to advance fundamental and applied science, access world-class capabilities and develop talent.

“At the commercial end, industrial partners must be integrated into the process to unlock funding and create markets. Importantly, we must scale up these innovations. If we do not scale them, they will remain research projects,” he said.

He described the journey between scientific discovery and commercial application as long and complex, arguing that closer cooperation could reduce both the time and risks involved in introducing new technologies.

“By combining fundamental scientific research, development, industrial expertise and engineering, we can accelerate innovation and significantly reduce the risks associated with new technologies. Partnerships are therefore not simply enablers of success – they are a precondition for success,” he said.

Transitioning in SA

South Africa’s transition, he said, was particularly difficult because it had to reduce emissions while continuing to pursue industrialisation, economic growth, competitiveness, inclusion and employment.

“These objectives may, at times, appear contradictory, but we believe they can be achieved together through the adoption of technology and innovation,” he said.

Sasol’s operations remain heavily dependent on coal, making decarbonisation both a commercial and societal necessity.

Mudzunga said the company’s strategy involves lowering emissions and operating costs while using the transition to establish new businesses.

“No single technology can decarbonise a complex industrial system such as ours. Success will require an integrated portfolio,” he said.

That portfolio, he explained, would include renewable power and feedstocks, greater process efficiency, digital technologies, carbon capture and storage, carbon valorisation and circular-economy initiatives.

“Rather than searching for a single cure or silver bullet, we must combine multiple solutions and deploy them strategically at scale. The energy transition will ultimately be achieved through an integrated approach, rather than through a single technology,” he said.

He said Sasol had already developed expertise that could support sustainable aviation fuel and other low-carbon products.

At the same time, its existing industrial facilities could reduce the capital required to scale emerging technologies.

However, future projects would have to be selected according to their feasibility and ability to compete commercially.

“The energy transition is one of the greatest challenges facing our society, but it is also one of our greatest opportunities.

“Through technology, collaboration and sustained innovation, we believe Sasol can play a meaningful role in building a more sustainable future,” he said.

text:
Center for Green Market Activation, RMI, and 3Degrees partner on new initiative to harness collective demand for green ammonia to reduce fertilizer production emissions.

WASHINGTON, Sept. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Today, the Center for Green Market Activation (GMA), RMI, and 3Degrees announced the launch of the Green Ammonia Buyers Alliance (GABA), a new initiative that will help food and beverage companies accelerate investment in green ammonia production to reduce emissions from fertilizer manufacturing.

The launch of GABA leverages the combined expertise and shared commitment of GMA, RMI, and 3Degrees to accelerate industrial decarbonization through innovative market-based solutions and extends a proven collective procurement approach into a sector primed to convert potential into impact. The program's founding members include leading companies within the food and beverage sector.

Ammonia production is one of the largest sources of emissions in fertilizer manufacturing. Green ammonia, produced using renewable electricity and water rather than natural gas, can eliminate nearly all emissions from this process. Accelerating its deployment represents one of the most significant and scalable opportunities to reduce emissions from the fertilizer value chain, which generates an estimated 1.2 gigatons of CO₂e annually. For food and beverage companies, investment in green ammonia offers a scalable pathway to materially reduce supply chain emissions while decreasing dependence on fossil-based fertilizers that are subject to significant price volatility.

Despite its potential to drive down emissions from fertilizer, green ammonia has proven difficult to scale. Dozens of projects have been announced around the world, but most still face the challenge of securing enough bankable demand to move forward. At the same time, food and beverage companies, many of whom have set ambitious Scope 3 emission reduction targets, sit five to six steps downstream from ammonia producers. This creates a gap between the projects seeking investment and the companies most interested in sourcing low-carbon inputs to address fertilizer-related emissions.

Through GABA, companies will be able to directly support the growth of the green ammonia-based fertilizer market, demonstrate the validity of green ammonia as a key fertilizer decarbonization solution, and advance progress toward their climate and supply chain sustainability goals.

"No company can scale a market like green ammonia on its own," said Kim Carnahan, GMA CEO. "GABA gives members of key sectors like food and bev a way to act collectively, creating the demand signal needed to help move projects from announcement to implementation."

By bringing companies together through a shared procurement process, GABA will aggregate demand for green ammonia and create a stronger market signal for producers, project developers, and investors. Through a book-and-claim system, member companies will purchase Environmental Attribute Certificates (EACs) directly from verified green ammonia producers, helping provide the revenue certainty needed to support new projects while enabling companies to address fertilizer production emissions that would otherwise remain out of reach.

"Green ammonia is one of the most important long-term pathways for reducing emissions from fertilizer production, but bringing new production online requires clear market signals," said Thomas Koch Blank, Managing Director at RMI. "The Green Ammonia Buyers Alliance builds on what we've learned across other sectors: when companies come together around credible, long-term demand, they can give producers and investors confidence to move projects forward and accelerate adoption of lower-emissions technologies."

For many companies, EACs offer the most practical and scalable pathway available today for addressing value chain emissions beyond their direct control. Recent developments in corporate climate guidance, including the SBTi Corporate Net-Zero Standard V2 and the Advanced and Indirect Mitigation (AIM) Platform Standard, provide increased clarity on how companies can account for and report these types of value chain interventions. GABA's approach mirrors similar market-based systems that have successfully channeled investment into renewable electricity, sustainable aviation fuel, decarbonized shipping, zero-emission heavy-duty trucking, and low-carbon construction materials.

GABA builds on growing momentum in fertilizer decarbonization and emerging demand for lower-emissions fertilizer solutions. Through the Low Carbon Fertilizer Alliance (LCFA), a 3Degrees-led global initiative comprising 25 food and beverage companies, companies have already begun leveraging market-based approaches to decarbonize large scale fertilizer plants through blue ammonia and nitric acid decarbonization.

"We're excited to partner with GMA and RMI to launch GABA and build on the growing momentum behind fertilizer decarbonization," said 3Degrees CEO Philippe Vedrenne. "GABA creates a dedicated platform for companies to collectively support the development of the green ammonia market. This platform directly compliments the Low Carbon Fertilizer Alliance, which is focused on retrofitting existing fertilizer production infrastructure through collective action."

By bringing together 3Degrees' expertise in environmental commodity markets and early work with fertilizer EACs alongside GMA and RMI's experience designing high-integrity book-and-claim systems and demand aggregation programs, GABA provides companies with a proven, credible pathway to support green ammonia production. Members will benefit from technical expertise, transparent market design, and a competitive procurement process intended to direct demand toward the most credible and impactful green ammonia projects at the most competitive cost possible for companies purchasing EACs.

GABA plans to launch its first pilot procurement in Q4 2026, giving participating companies an opportunity to help establish one of the first collective demand signals for green ammonia-based fertilizers. Buyers engaged in GABA's inaugural procurement will have unique opportunities to inform program design and capture first-mover discounts through 2027. Companies interested in joining GABA or learning more about upcoming procurement opportunities are encouraged to contact fertilizer@gmacenter.org.

Media inquiries please contact:

Alison Greene, Center for Green Market Activation: alison.greene@gmacenter.org

About the Center for Green Market Activation

The Center for Green Market Activation (GMA) is a US-based, globally focused non-profit. Through innovative procurement approaches and sector-specific buyers alliances, GMA catalyzes and scales the uptake of low-carbon goods and services within carbon-intensive industries including aviation, maritime, trucking, cement and concrete, and chemicals. With collective decades of experience in environmental markets and alternative fuels and materials, the GMA team works to standardize new, green markets and forges mutually beneficial partnerships between climate-focused companies, suppliers, and mission-aligned non-profit organizations to channel funding to critical climate technologies in pursuit of accelerated sectoral decarbonization. Learn more at gmacenter.org.

About RMI

Rocky Mountain Institute (RMI) is an independent, nonpartisan nonprofit founded in 1982 that transforms global energy systems through market-driven solutions to secure a prosperous, resilient, clean energy future for all. In collaboration with businesses, policymakers, funders, communities, and other partners, RMI drives investment to scale clean energy solutions, reduce energy waste, and boost access to affordable clean energy in ways that enhance security, strengthen the economy, and improve people's livelihoods. RMI is active in over 50 countries.

About 3Degrees

3Degrees, a Certified B Corporation, makes it possible for climate-conscious organizations to take urgent action on climate change. As a trusted partner in global supply chain decarbonization, 3Degrees delivers renewable energy solutions, carbon project development, and high-integrity Scope 3 strategies. In 2024, 3Degrees founded the Low Carbon Fertilizer Alliance (LCFA), aggregating corporate demand to de-risk and scale factory-level emissions reductions across complex agricultural value chains. Learn more at 3degreesinc.com.

title: TAROM's first Boeing 737 MAX signals the start of a long-awaited fleet renewal programme
description:
First Boeing 737 MAX 8 delivered to TAROM The first aircraft arrived in Bucharest after being ferried from Seattle via Keflavík in Iceland.
TAROM will fly its 737 MAX fleet on routes connecting Bucharest with major European capitals, “providing an enhanced passenger experience,” according to the carrier.
TAROM originally announced an order for five Boeing 737 MAX 8s on July 16, 2018, in a deal valued by Boeing at $586 million at list prices.
Under the restructuring programme, TAROM ultimately planned to introduce four 737 MAX 8s through a mixture of operating and financial leases.
Marking the start of a fleet revitalisation For TAROM, the significance of the 737 MAX goes beyond the arrival of a single new aircraft.
text:
Romania’s national airline, TAROM, has entered a new chapter with the arrival of its first Boeing 737 MAX 8, marking the beginning of a major fleet refresh intended to make the carrier smaller, more efficient and more competitive.

The new aircraft, registered YR-BGO and named Mircea Lucescu, was formally delivered to TAROM on 12 September 2026 and is the first 737 MAX to enter service with a Romanian airline.

First Boeing 737 MAX 8 delivered to TAROM

The first aircraft arrived in Bucharest after being ferried from Seattle via Keflavík in Iceland. A second MAX is expected to follow shortly, with the four-aircraft programme scheduled to be completed by 2027. TAROM has also indicated that it is looking beyond those four aircraft, with discussions around potentially adding another MAX later in the decade.

The new aircraft is particularly significant because TAROM has been operating a relatively small and ageing fleet while undergoing a substantial restructuring. TAROM will fly its 737 MAX fleet on routes connecting Bucharest with major European capitals, “providing an enhanced passenger experience,” according to the carrier.

The arrival of the airline’s new 737 MAX 8 is not simply an additional aircraft but represents the replacement of older-generation Boeing narrowbodies and is central to a plan to simplify the fleet, reduce operating costs, and better compete with the likes of Wizz Air, HiSky, AnimaWings and Ryanair in the Romanian market.

TAROM’s current fleet illustrates why renewal is necessary. Before the MAX’s arrival, the carrier’s mainline fleet consisted of Boeing 737-700s and 737-800s alongside ATR 72 turboprops.

Current fleet data shows three 737-700s, four 737-800s, two ATR 72-500s, and four ATR 72-600s. The 737-700s, in particular, are among the aircraft targeted for replacement by the new-generation MAX.

The fleet is vastly different from TAROM’s larger operation of previous decades. Indeed, the European Commission’s restructuring documentation describes how the airline had a fleet of 29 aircraft before the rationalisation programme, including Boeing 737-300s and 737-700s, Airbus A318s, and a sizeable ATR fleet.

The restructuring plan envisaged reducing that fleet substantially while concentrating operations around a smaller number of aircraft types.

This first arrival has been much anticipated

The MAX order itself has had a long history, with the delivery of the first aircraft much anticipated. TAROM originally announced an order for five Boeing 737 MAX 8s on July 16, 2018, in a deal valued by Boeing at $586 million at list prices. At the time, the aircraft were expected to be delivered over the following years.

The programme subsequently became entangled with TAROM’s financial difficulties, restructuring and the wider disruption to the aviation industry. Rather than simply receiving the five aircraft originally announced, the current fleet-renewal plan has evolved around leased aircraft.

In 2024, TAROM and CDB Aviation announced agreements covering two new 737 MAX 8s from CDB Aviation’s Boeing orderbook. Those aircraft were originally scheduled for delivery between December 2025 and January 2026 and were to be configured with 189 seats.

Under the restructuring programme, TAROM ultimately planned to introduce four 737 MAX 8s through a mixture of operating and financial leases. The European Commission described the MAX as replacing the airline’s outgoing 737-700s and helping create a more streamlined and uniform fleet.

The objective was not just to acquire newer aircraft, but to achieve lower operating costs, greater efficiency and a more consistent passenger product.

That makes the first MAX especially important. Boeing says the 737-8 offers roughly 20% lower fuel consumption and carbon emissions than the aircraft it replaces, while giving TAROM a modern narrowbody capable of operating both domestic and European routes efficiently.

Marking the start of a fleet revitalisation

For TAROM, the significance of the 737 MAX goes beyond the arrival of a single new aircraft. It is the visible beginning of a fleet transformation that has been years in the making.

The carrier is moving away from a heterogeneous fleet assembled over several generations towards a smaller, more standardised operation built around modern Boeing 737s and ATR turboprops.

The challenge will be turning that new equipment into sustainable growth. TAROM remains in the middle of a restructuring programme, and its relatively small fleet leaves little room for operational disruption.

But the arrival of the MAX gives the Romanian flag carrier an important tool for the next phase – a modern, fuel-efficient aircraft capable of replacing some of its oldest narrowbodies while improving efficiency across its European network. After years of waiting, TAROM’s fleet renewal is finally becoming tangible.

text:
Dubai: Etihad Airways CEO Antonoaldo Neves has one major concern as the airline heads into the final months of 2026: jet fuel prices. Demand is not keeping him awake. Fuel is.

“I think jet fuel keeps me awake,” Neves told Gulf News on the sidelines of the opening day of the Arabian Travel Market in Dubai, as the Abu Dhabi airline continues to expand its fleet, network and workforce.

For Neves, the biggest risk facing Etihad is not demand but the cost of jet fuel — and what sustained high prices could mean for airfares next year.

He said the key question for Etihad is now what happens to the average fare next year if jet fuel prices remain elevated, particularly as airlines across the Gulf, Europe and the US compete heavily for passengers.

“So we compete a lot, right? And every time you compete a lot, the competition level is high. You cannot pass on prices as easy as you are in other markets.”

“If you ask me, what is my thinking right now in terms of risk challenge? It’s what’s going to happen with the average fare next year because of jet fuel price,” he said.

Jet fuel was around $170 a barrel, according to the International Air Transport Association's (IATA) jet fuel monitor, according to Neves, who said the crack spread — the difference between the price of crude oil and refined products such as jet fuel — was also high.

However, he said the forward curve was indicating a less severe picture than current prices and argued that the present spike was unlikely to be sustainable.

“I hope jet fuel price goes back to normal levels,” he said. “The forward curve is saying that the jet fuel forward curve is not great, but it’s not as bad as the jet fuel right now.”

Neves pointed to the sharp move in fuel prices during the recent regional disruption as evidence of how quickly the market can change.

“We had the situation about six months ago, right? And jet fuel went back to 110 in July, so it’s going to come back. It’s not sustainable, right? So it’s just volatility because of the situation, the global situation.”

Fuel concern

Etihad is partly protected by fuel hedging, but it remains exposed to movements in the market. Neves said the current fuel environment is being driven by a wider global situation, rather than the Middle East alone, pointing to developments in Russia and Ukraine as factors that are also affecting oil prices.

“I hope jet fuel price goes back to normal levels,” he said, adding that the current situation was not sustainable. He said the forward curve suggested prices could eventually ease, although the airline still has to manage the impact of current prices.

For passengers, the key question is whether higher fuel costs will eventually appear in ticket prices.

Neves said that will depend partly on how much pricing power individual airlines have. Stronger airlines could benefit if fares rise, while weaker carriers that cannot generate enough demand could come under greater pressure.

“Elasticity plays,” he said. However, he cautioned against trying to predict exactly how the market will respond, saying conditions can change quickly, as airlines experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Flights full

For now, Etihad is seeing strong demand, with Neves repeatedly describing the airline’s flights as “full, full, full”.

The carrier’s load factor reached 92 per cent last month, he said, despite several international travel advisories remaining in place.

Etihad’s flights from Europe to the UAE are full, while its services from the US are also performing strongly, said the CEO. The airline is preparing to launch Calgary as it continues rebuilding and expanding its network.

“I understand countries take time to remove travel advisories,” Neves said. But he believes travellers are increasingly making their own decisions based on the experiences of friends and other passengers who have already travelled to the UAE.

“People understand that governments take longer to remove these travel advisories,” he said. “If you want to travel, their friends travel and they say, ‘OK, travel. It was great.’”

He also pointed to Etihad’s operational performance during the disruption, saying the airline did not cancel flights at the last minute or move customers away from services.

“Word of mouth, and I think the great track record that we have in these situations also help,” he said.

More flights

Etihad is now operating 320 flights a day, which Neves said is 20 per cent more than last year. The airline spent the first three months of the year gradually bringing capacity back, moving through 30 per cent, 40 per cent and 70 per cent levels before reaching 100 per cent capacity by July.

The past three months have been particularly strong.

In July, Etihad had 17 per cent more capacity than in July 2025, while the airline also made more money that month than it did in July last year.

August was slightly weaker because of fuel prices, but Neves said the performance across July and August gave Etihad “strength and certainty that the strategy is in the right place”.

September has also started strongly, with the CEO saying the airline's flights are continuing to fill up.

Fleet doubles

The airline is continuing to expand rapidly, with Etihad expecting to finish this year with around 140 aircraft, compared with 70 in 2022.

“In four years we doubled the number of aircraft,” Neves said. “We’re really proud of that. I don’t know any other airline in the world our size that has doubled in four years.”

Around 15 aircraft are due to arrive in the second half of this year. The majority are narrow-body aircraft, while the airline is also expecting A350s and other wide-body aircraft.

Several of the incoming narrow-bodies will be A321LRs, which have become an important part of Etihad’s network strategy. And for Etihad investing in newer-generation aircraft that consume less fuel is a more immediate and practical route to improving efficiency.

“The most important thing I can do is to invest in new aircraft type to burn less fuel per flight per hour,” he said, adding that new-generation aircraft can use about 20 per cent less fuel per passenger.

“There is no sustainable aviation fuel in the world that can solve for that.”

Etihad spends about $2 billion a year on new aircraft, while its annual fuel bill is also around $2 billion, Neves said. "Whenever SAF is available, and whenever SAF is is at the right market price, we we can buy it," said the aviation veteran.

China, Africa

The aircraft arriving now are also helping Etihad prepare for another phase of growth, with China and Africa set to be major areas of focus next year. “Everywhere is important, but we stagger the growth so that we can focus,” Neves said. “So next year is China and Africa.”

The airline is using the A321LR to help increase frequencies as well as serve longer routes. Neves said Etihad now has double-daily services to almost all destinations in Europe, while Bangkok has reached five flights a day.

He said the narrow-body aircraft makes those frequencies possible and allows the airline to offer more choice to passengers without relying exclusively on larger wide-body aircraft.

“Schedule and frequency is a very important part of a product,” he said.

Break-even target

Despite the rapid expansion, Etihad is targeting a break-even result this year. Neves said the airline could make a small profit or lose a small amount depending on fuel-price volatility, but stressed that profitability is not the main priority for 2026.

“The most important thing this year is cash flow generation,” he said.

The airline needs to generate cash to fund its capital spending, including new aircraft, while Neves said Etihad is in a comfortable financial position with a strong balance sheet and “almost zero” bank debt.

“We’re going to get stronger out of the situation,” he said.

Hiring drive

The expansion is also creating jobs. Etihad hired more than 600 people during March, April and May, including pilots and cabin crew, and Neves said the airline expects to add another 600 employees during the second half of the year.

The longer-term hiring plan is considerably bigger.

Etihad expects to hire around 1,500 people every year for the next five years, as it continues adding aircraft to its fleet.

“We’re adding 20 planes per year every year,” Neves said, explaining that each aircraft requires around 60 to 70 additional employees.

Around 200 of those annual hires would be pilots, he said.

Premium push

A major takeaway? It is evident that Etihad is propping up its premium segment in a big way. Neves’ comments came as Etihad unveiled its new-look seats and wider Beyond Borders customer experience at ATM on Monday.

Neves said the airline is putting a major emphasis on premium travel as it looks to move the customer experience into its next generation.
